extracted.intended_audience: clergy, theologians, educated readers debating Christianity and religious apologetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing the quality, evidence, and rhetoric of sermons and apologetic arguments about Christianity; focuses on standards of proof, use of rhetoric, authenticity of texts, and proper conduct of intellectual inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful and serious examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Christianity 'deserves at least respectful, and serious attention' and should be 'thoroughly examined' because if it is from God its truth is of the highest importance to mankind, and if it is not from God it ought to be rejected as either error or fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons given: (1) If from God, its truth must be investigated for human welfare; (2) If not from God, it must be rejected (either delusion or deception). Also merits examination on account of the moral character of its founder. Treat the subject 'coolly, and respectfully' and be prepared to investigate deliberate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sound reasoning to wit and ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments in defence of or against religion should rely on reasoning rather than 'sarcasm, abuse, and sneer' or mere wit and satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: attacking religion 'merely with wit, and ridicule' is weak. While ridicule can wound, a cause that claims to withstand investigation should meet substantive argument. Note: the author acknowledges clergy sometimes use ridicule (e.g., Warburton) and that fairness permits both parties to employ satire, but the stronger standard is sound logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocates must welcome open inquiry and not demand convenient framing
rubrics_metrics.description: If a cause claims to be able to sustain deliberate investigation, its advocates should not shrink from examination nor insist opponents present arguments in a form most convenient for the advocate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: demanding that an opponent arrange objections in a specific, convenient form (compares to insisting an opposing lawyer arrange objections to suit the advocate). Openness to candid, patient enquiry is the mark of a claim confident in its reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on 'rumour' or popularity as foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A rumour' is not an adequate foundation on which to build a religion; popular expectation alone does not prove prophetic fulfillment or divine origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate historical causes that could produce widespread expectation (e.g., social conditions among Jews under Roman oppression). Check whether the 'rumour' existed contemporaneously with the figure in question or arose later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic fulfillment must match the specified marks, not merely resemble
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing a single or a few characteristics similar to prophecy is insufficient; prophecies list many marks and fulfillment requires meeting those marks, not only some agreeable traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the characteristic 'teaching and enlightening the Gentiles' is only one among many marks; even if it applied, it would not be sufficient proof. Comparative example: Muhammad arguably better fulfilled that single characteristic in his life than Jesus did, so singular correspondences are weak evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require strong historical testimony for supernatural claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Supernatural events (miracles) demand as much historical evidence for their authenticity as we require for major historical facts (e.g., deaths of Pompey or Julius Caesar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the quantity and quality of contemporaneous testimony, provenance of documents, contradictions among accounts, and whether later fathers' quotations clearly refer to the canonical texts. The author claims we have far less robust testimony for gospel miracles than for well-attested classical events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity of proponents is not proof of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The sincerity or honesty of those who propagate a belief does not constitute proof that the belief is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: inferring truth from the apostolic or missionary zeal of proponents. The author stresses that honest belief by advocates (even apostles) is insufficient evidence of the truth of their doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid appeals to sentiment and consequences when judging truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to feeling, to the beneficial consequences of belief, or to fear of consequences if belief is false, are irrelevant to the question of truth and unfair in preparing auditors for inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of improper tactics: describing historical atrocities to bias listeners, arguing that Christianity must be true because its denial would leave people without comfort. The author insists the consequences of a system being false do not affect its truth and that reason, not sentiment, should guide judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize the authenticity, authorship, and textual integrity of New Testament books
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims based on gospel or epistolary testimony require examination of who authored those texts, whether they are eyewitness accounts, whether they are compilations from earlier documents, and whether interpolations or contradictions exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific issues raised: Luke is not an eyewitness (hearsay); the three first gospels may be compilations from anonymous earlier documents; the Book of Acts was rejected by some early Christian groups and may reflect a partisan pro-Pauline account; certain Pauline epistles have been argued apocryphal. Consult scholarship (e.g., Marsh, Michaelis) and be wary of later interpolations and contested canonicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret apostles' expectations in historical context—beware retrospective spiritualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the apostles themselves expected a temporal, national restoration (a carnal kingdom) rather than the later 'spiritual' interpretation; their original beliefs affect how their testimony should be read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited evidence: passages in Luke and Acts where apostles ask 'Lord, wilt thou now restore the kingdom to Israel?' and post-resurrection statements implying expectation of near return. Implication: if apostles expected a near, temporal fulfillment and that failed, this affects the credibility and evolution of doctrines (e.g., disappearance of Jewish Christians).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not defend falsehoods for their utility ('no pious fraud')
rubrics_metrics.description: It is absurd and immoral to defend an unsound foundation on the principle that it is useful; usefulness does not justify deliberate deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author invokes moral duty: truth in the long run is more useful than error (quoting Lord Bacon). Anti-pattern: 'we must tolerate or promote a lie because it produces comfort or social order' is condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question late canonization and authority claims of church fathers
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the New Testament canon was collected and established centuries after the apostles (and largely by Gentile Christians), one should be cautious about treating later ecclesiastical declarations as definitive proof of authenticity or authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points to consider: early diversity of Christian texts (e.g., Gospel of the Twelve, Pastor of Hermas, Book of Enoch), disagreements among early churches, selective survivals of anti-Christian critics' fragments, and practices by some Fathers (e.g., alleged allowance of falsehoods in polemics). Use critical historical methods rather than relying on later ecclesiastical sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public worship and moral precepts can be independent of New Testament claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejecting the New Testament does not necessarily leave one without religion or moral law; the Old Testament (or Theism) and pre-existing public worship suffice for moral instruction and social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: when debating the necessity or truth of the New Testament, separate questions of public worship, morality, and social religion from claims specifically grounded on New Testament truth.
